summaries.text: We're introducing basic terminology: an algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, while a program is its implementation in any programming language. A data structure is the way we organise data for effective use by a program.

The course will focus on exploring various data structures and using them to solve algorithmic problems. An algorithmic problem is defined as having a specified input and no output specification, requiring students to develop an algorithm that meets certain criteria.

We're considering various possible input instances to an algorithmic problem, each of which can be formed from a sequence of sorted non-decreasing numbers. The lecturer is now discussing the notion of a "good algorithm" in the context of multiple possible solutions to a problem.

A good algorithm is considered efficient, with small running time and low memory usage, which will be the two measures of efficiency considered in this course. We will focus on how the running time of an algorithm increases with the size of the input.

The running time of an algorithm increases unpredictably with the size of the input, and this behaviour is also of interest to us. We will measure running time through an experimental study by implementing the algorithm, using different data sets of varying sizes and composition, and then timing how long it takes to run.

You use a system utility to measure the time taken by the program, not a physical stopwatch. The experimental study has limitations, including the need to implement the algorithm and the inability to test an infinite number of inputs.

When comparing algorithms, it's essential to use the same hardware and software environments to get accurate results. A methodology is being developed to help analyse running times without needing to implement or test the algorithms themselves.

The methodology will allow for the evaluation of an algorithm's efficiency regardless of the environment or platform, by taking into account all possible input instances. The course will use pseudocode to specify algorithms, with an example being the algorithm that finds the maximum element in an array.

The pseudocode is using high-level constructs to specify an algorithm that finds the maximum element in an array, with a variable called current max being used to keep track of the maximum value seen so far. The algorithm will run through the remaining elements of the array, comparing each one with the current maximum element.

If the current maximum element is less than the current element being considered, current max will be updated to that element. The pseudocode will use standard numeric and Boolean expressions, with a different assignment operator, a left arrow, instead of the usual equals sign.

The pseudocode will use a different assignment operator, a left arrow, and the equality operator will be a single equals sign. Programming constructs such as if-then-else statements, while loops, and return values will also be used in a clear and explicit manner.

The lecturer is now explaining how to analyze algorithms by identifying primitive operations in the pseudocode, which include low-level operations such as data movement and arithmetic or logical operations. These primitive operations are then counted in the pseudocode to determine the time complexity of the algorithm.

The lecturer is now inspecting the pseudocode to count the number of primitive operations executed by the algorithm, as this will determine the time complexity. The lecturer is using the example of sorting to illustrate this process, highlighting that the output must be a permutation of the input in non-decreasing order.

The running time of a sorting algorithm depends on the number of elements, how sorted they are, and which algorithm is used. The lecturer is introducing a common real-world analogy for sorting, using a hand of cards.

The lecturer is explaining the insertion sort technique, where each new card is inserted at the correct position in the hand, like inserting an 8 between 7 and 9. The pseudo-code for insertion sort is being described as taking an array of integers as input and producing a sorted permutation of the original numbers as output.

The array will be sorted from A1 through Ai at any point in time, with A1 through Aj minus 1 being sorted and the jth element being inserted into the correct position. The index i will be used to help insert the key into the sorted sequence A1 through Aj minus 1.

The index i is running down from j minus 1 to 1 in a while loop, decreasing i. The loop compares each element with the key 7 and moves the larger elements to the right to make space for the key in the correct position.

The loop will terminate when it finds an element less than the key or when i equals 0, at which point the key will be inserted at the beginning. The element being inserted is shifted one step to the right as each larger element is moved to make space for it.

The algorithm will insert the key at the index i plus 1, shifting elements to the right as necessary. The lecturer is now moving on to analyze the algorithm, counting the primitive operations involved.

The lecturer is counting the number of primitive operations involved, identifying three operations in the current code segment. The operations are assigned variables c1 to c6 to represent their respective times, with some operations executed n times in the entire program.

The lecturer explains that the operation represented by variable j is counted as n times, but with small potential errors. The operation is then broken down into two cases: it is done n times for one part and n-1 times for the rest.

T sub j represents the number of times an element must be shifted to the right when inserting the jth card into the hand. The total number of times the while loop condition is seen is the sum of T sub j from j=2 to n.

The while loop condition is seen one more time than the last iteration of the while loop, which is why T sub j is j minus 1. The constant assignment is done exactly n minus 1 times as part of the for loop.
T sub j depends on the instance of numbers and is always 1 if the input is already sorted, either in increasing or decreasing order.

When trying to insert the jth element into a decreasingly ordered array, T sub j will be equal to j as it compares with all other j elements. This results in a running time of n squared, behaving more like n squared.

In the best case, the total time is roughly n times a constant, making it a linear time algorithm. In the average case, you would expect to compare against half the elements, resulting in a time complexity of roughly n squared divided by 4.

The lecturer is explaining the different cases of algorithmic time complexity, stating that the worst case is the maximum possible time for any instance of a given size. The worst case time is defined as the maximum possible time that the algorithm would take for any instance of a given size, regardless of the input.

The lecturer is explaining that if we plot the worst case, best case, and average case times for inputs of all sizes, the plots will be monotonically increasing. This is because the time taken by an algorithm will always increase as the input size increases.

The worst case scenario is most often used because it provides an upper bound on the algorithm's time complexity, giving a clear indication of its maximum time requirement. For many algorithms, the worst case is also frequently encountered, often resulting in average case times being comparable to worst case times.

The running time of an algorithm is typically evaluated in the worst case, as it's a harder quantity to work with than average case time. Asymptotic analysis focuses on eliminating superficial details to compare algorithms with the same time complexity, such as n squared.

The constant factor in an algorithm's time complexity is typically dependent on hardware and other factors, and is therefore not of interest in asymptotic analysis. What matters is how the running time increases with the size of the input, specifically the rate at which it increases, which is captured by asymptotic analysis.

The running time of an algorithm is being compared to how it increases with input size using asymptotic analysis, specifically with Big O notation. Big O notation is being defined as saying a function f of n is Big O of another function g of n, where both functions are non-decreasing as input size increases.

The functions f of n and g of n are non-decreasing, and f of n is Big O of g of n if there exists a constant c and n0 such that f of n is less than c times g of n for n larger than n0. The lecturer illustrates this concept using two functions, f of n = 2n + 6 and g of n = n, where f of n is shown to be Big O of g of n.
The function f of n = 2n + 6 is always larger than g of n = n. We find that the constant c is 4, and n0 is the point where 2n + 6 crosses 4n.
The constant c is 4 and the point of crossing, where 4n becomes larger than 2n + 6, is at n = 3. This makes f of n, which is 2n + 6, big O of n.

g of n is also O of n because it is just n plus a constant. The lecturer is arguing that n squared is not O of n because no constant c can be found to make n squared less than c times n for large enough n.
To determine if a function is big O of another, one drops all constants and lower order terms. For example, the function 50n log n is big O of n log n because its highest order term is n log n.

The sum of terms is less than a constant times n square log n for sufficiently large n. This function 50n log n is also big O of n to the 5, but we prefer to call it big O of n log n for a tighter bound.

We will use big O notation to express the number of primitive operations executed by an algorithm as a function of the input size. An algorithm with big O of n is considered better than one with big O of n square because its running time increases more slowly with larger inputs.
An algorithm with a big O of log n running time is better than one with big O of n, and it's also better than n square and n cube, but worse than 2 to the power of n.

The running time of big O n is better than 2 n square in very large instances, but smaller instances may have different performance. We will now use a pseudocode example to practice asymptotic analysis.

The lecturer is illustrating asymptotic analysis with a pseudocode example of a for loop that computes each element a_i of an array a by summing the elements x_j from x_0 to x_i and dividing by (i + 1). The loop iterates over the array, using j as the running index, to calculate each a_i.

The step being repeated is executed n^2 times, which is its dominant characteristic, making it a less efficient algorithm. This is because the loop iterates over the array n times, and within each iteration, the step is executed once.
The algorithm's running time is dominated by the step being executed n^2 times. A potential improvement involves keeping a running sum of the x_i values, rather than recalculating it every time.

The algorithm is repeatedly calculating the sum of prefixes, which is inefficient, so we are keeping an accumulator variable to store the running sum. This accumulator is updated in each iteration of the loop, taking only two primitive operations per run.

The algorithm's efficiency is being classified as linear because it takes order n time, with each iteration taking two primitive operations. The lecturer is introducing other time complexity terms, including logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential, in addition to linear, quadratic, and big O notation.

The lecturer is explaining the big omega notation, which provides a lower bound, and defines a function as omega of g of n if it is greater than or equal to a constant times g of n from a certain point onwards. The big theta notation is also introduced, where a function is theta of g of n if it is bounded above and below by constants times g of n.

A function f of n is theta of g of n if it is bounded above and below by constant times g of n, or equivalently if it is both big o of g of n and omega of g of n. The lecturer is now introducing the little o and little omega notations, which are non-tight analogues of big o and big omega.

The lecturer is explaining that big o and big omega notations can be thought of as "less than or equal to" and "greater than or equal to" relationships between functions. Little o and little omega notations are non-tight analogues that represent "strictly less than" and "strictly greater than" relationships respectively.

Little o and little omega notations represent strictly less than and strictly greater than relationships, respectively. The formal definition of little o is that for every constant c, there should exist some n0 such that f of n is less than c times g of n for n more than n0.

The lecturer is listing examples of problem sizes that can be solved in one second, one minute, and one hour, with the largest problem size being around 2500. This illustrates how different running times can affect the size of problems that can be solved, with larger constants allowing larger problem sizes.

The lecturer explains how different running times affect the size of problems that can be solved, with linear time allowing huge increases, n log n a large increase, n square a small increase, and 2 to the n almost no increase in problem size. An algorithm with a running time of 2 to the n can only solve problems of size 100 or less.
